5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

draft/05-background.md:3:Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
draft/05-background.md:7:The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.

A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, so ambient air enters the chamber continuously. Air is withdrawn fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the left.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a depiction convention for this sheet only. The body and the band are the whole of the machine drawn on this sheet.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as a broad strip between that underside and the tile; the depth of the strip is shown schematically and no particular proportion is asserted. The band stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile with no gap, and the machine hides the stretch of tile behind it. An open stretch of tile lies in front of the machine, down to the near edge of the tile.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path, in the manner of a loose cord: a single continuous curved line of the same line weight as the outlines of the machine, drawn as one stroke along its whole length. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place being shown schematically with no attachment formation shown, and runs away to the left, sagging gently over the open expanse of tile, and its free end is the point at which that single line stops, well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area. It stays clear of the machine and of the open stretch of tile in front of the machine.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, the rectangular body with its band. Identified well inside the front face of the rectangular body, above the band and away from the flexible pulling element 46.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band under the rectangular body. Identified well inside the broad front strip of the band, below the underside of the rectangular body and above the tile, clear of both of those boundaries.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is that slack curved path. Identified on the path where it runs over the open expanse of tile, clear of the machine.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside that open stretch of tile in front of the machine, clear of the machine and of the flexible pulling element 46.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 24, 36, 46

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 24
- 36
- 46

All five sheet failures are addressed in the figure briefs, with the drawing descriptions and detailed description kept in step. One thing worth flagging: partway through this turn my first pass of figure edits was rolled back on disk (the five figure files and `draft/07-drawings.md` reverted to their pre-repair content while the detailed-description edit persisted). I re-applied them and verified the final on-disk state.

**FIG. 1** (leader failures on 10, 12, 24): the sheet was carrying seven numerals on crowded, thin geometry, which is what produced the 0.5 and 0.2 unit clearances and sent numeral 12 into the open area of the handle ring. I redistributed rather than deleted: the sheet now carries 10, 36, 44 on a machine drawn as one plain body with a band and a grip, and numeral 10 gets a broad interior target on the body's front face instead of the narrow front-left corner line the reviewers kept rejecting. Base 12, motor 18, mechanism 20, and perimeter member 24 keep their labels on FIG. 2, which now shows the motor as a second unhatched housing (seven numerals, within the limit). The band and body on FIG. 1 are described generically, with no canonical part name or numeral, as the redistribution rules require.

**FIG. 2 and FIG. 4** (hatch direction and chevron findings): the per-body hatch angles were invented rendering constraints, not disclosure-grounded geometry, so I removed them. Both sheets now positively require regularly spaced straight parallel hatching lines on each cut body, and the bands are identified by stacking order rather than by hatch pattern.

**FIG. 3** (numeral 24 rejected cluster): the ring band is now required to be broad along each of its four sides, and 24's target was widened from "the straight left-hand side" to any place well inside the band between its outer and inner edges.

**FIG. 5** (cord drawn as a two-edge ribbon with a rounded cap): the pulling element is now specified positively as a single continuous curved line of the same weight as the machine outlines, drawn as one stroke, its free end being the point where that line stops. Numeral 10 also moved from an outline target to a broad interior one. The brief was trimmed back to 2745 characters after the addition.

Verified on disk: all sixteen numerals in `draft/numerals.md` still appear across the sheets (10, 36, 44 / 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 36 / 16, 24 / 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 / 10, 24, 36, 46), no sheet exceeds seven numerals, every brief is under 2800 characters, each part name used on a sheet matches that sheet's numeral list, and no em dash, note, or placeholder appears anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`. Claims, numeral table, and the substance of the description are untouched.

reasoning: FIG. 1 carried seven numerals on geometry that could not support them: two housings, a grip and a thin band left numeral 12 with 0.5 units of clearance, numeral 24 with 0.2, and pushed 12's marker into the open area of the handle ring. Rather than fight the same crowded sheet again I applied the redistribution rule: FIG. 1 keeps 10, 36 and 44, and base 12, vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20 and perimeter member 24 are labelled on FIG. 2. Nothing was deleted, no numeral definition was dropped, and the union of the five sheets still covers all sixteen numerals in draft/numerals.md.

Numeral 10 is the assembly numeral, and the old brief sent it to the upright front-left corner line of the machine, which three reviewers read as landing on a housing instead. On FIG. 1 the machine is now one plain body with an unnumbered band and the grip, so 10 has a broad interior target on the body's front face with no competing numeral on that surface. This is the same construction that already passed semantic review on FIG. 5, where I likewise moved 10 from an outline target to the interior.

FIG. 2 gained the vibration motor as a second unhatched housing so that numeral 18 keeps a home after leaving FIG. 1. That put the sheet at seven numerals, within the eight-numeral limit, and required two synchronizations in the text: the FIG. 2 entry in the Brief Description of the Drawings no longer says the motor is omitted, and the detailed description now says the motor is coupled to the first side 14 as seen in FIG. 2. Neither change touches the invention; both keep the text from asserting a part is visible on a sheet that does not list it.

The hatch-direction findings on FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 were caused by constraints I should not have written in the first place. Nothing in the disclosure specifies hatch angles for the base, perimeter member, covering element, bonding material or substrate, so directions such as rising to the right at 45 degrees and falling to the right at a shallow slope were invented rendering controls. I removed them and replaced them with the positive requirement that each cut body be filled with regularly spaced straight parallel hatching lines. That also disposes of the chevron finding on the bonding material, since the requirement is now stated as straight parallel lines rather than a direction the renderer kept missing. The bands remain identifiable by stacking order, uppermost, middle and lowest, which is how their numeral targets already read.

For FIG. 3 the marked-endpoint cluster for numeral 24 was rejected because the drawn ring band was too narrow to hold a grounded point. I strengthened the geometry positively, requiring the inner rectangle to stand well in from all four sides so the band reads plainly as a surface of its own, and I removed the left-hand-side restriction from 24's target so any place well inside the band between its outer and inner edges qualifies. A broader admissible region is what the endpoint rule asks for.

FIG. 5's cord was rendered as a two-edge ribbon with a rounded cap. The guidance forbids defining a cord by counting outline strokes or as a white-interior strip, so I described it positively: one continuous curved line of the same weight as the machine outlines, drawn as one stroke along its whole length, its free end being the point at which that line stops. Adding that language pushed the brief to 2928 characters, so I trimmed redundant tile and band description to bring it back to 2745.

I made no change to the claims, the numeral table, or any disclosed embodiment. The only text edits outside figures/ were the two FIG. entries in the Brief Description of the Drawings and one added figure cross-reference in the detailed description, both of which describe what the sheets show rather than what the invention is. The rendered pixels drove none of the substance: where the image model drew a ribbon or the wrong hatching, I corrected the brief rather than letting the drawing dictate the text.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn. Every edit was to figure briefs, two Brief Description of the Drawings entries, and one figure cross-reference, none of which bears on scope. The separation drafted earlier stands: DE-202021002652-U1 vibrates shafts carrying rubber-elastic suction cups, so its holding interface is compliant, while claim 1 requires every member of the motor-to-bearing-face path to be rigid with no elastomeric, foam or resilient mount interposed. US-11408462-B2 forms the wall of its decompressed space from elastic partitions and adds a frame member only to stop the partition collapsing inward. US-10001245-B2 abandons its vacuum coupling to move, switching the same generator to blower mode to float on an air cushion, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous. US-4934475-A seals its pressure-reduction space and uses vibration to reduce the suction-adhering force so the body can travel, the opposite function to delivering vibration through the hold into the covering element. US-11247858-B2 is peripheral and is cited for what it actually teaches, a suction plate that lifts sheet articles and sweeps debris. The feature carrying the claim clear of all five remains the deliberate non-sealing clearance combined with an extraction rate that sustains sub-atmospheric pressure despite continuous ingress.
